prize_parts.citation: for determining the atomic structure of nitrogenase and its iron-molybdenum cofactor, revealing how biology activates dinitrogen
for the development of base editing, programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: My opening first choice remains nitrogenase (B064). The crystal structures of the MoFe protein and its FeMo cofactor, culminating in the high-resolution identification of the interstitial light atom as a carbide, are a textbook case of structure explaining function in a metal cluster that performs one of the hardest reactions in nature. The structures were determined, not inferred, have been independently reproduced and refined over more than three decades, and underpin synthetic cluster and catalyst design relevant to ammonia chemistry. I am pairing it with base editing (B011) in a two-part prize because the discussion shows that B011 has the broadest support across the committee and is a genuinely different kind of achievement, an enabling chemical method used by a whole community, which is the other category of work I value. Together the two parts honour one structural-mechanistic landmark and one design-driven tool, and the union of three people (Rees, Einsle, Liu) is clean.
statement.case_against: For nitrogenase, the catalytic mechanism and the substrate-binding mode are still only partly resolved, and I am the only member who ranked it first, so I must accept that the case rests on a structure-centred motivation rather than a full mechanism. Dropping Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe leaves out real kinetic and biochemical contributors, which is an uncomfortable attribution cost. For base editing, the chemical novelty over existing deaminase and CRISPR tools is arguable, the 2020 prize is a precedent that cuts against it, and Komor, Gaudelli, Nishida and Kondo are all left out of a Liu-only part. Pairing two unrelated achievements could also be criticised as a compromise rather than a principled prize.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks base editing first as a new class of tool with immediate, widely used consequences, with Liu as the clear originator and Komor and Gaudelli as lead experimentalists, and says the protein-evolution chemistry fits the Chemistry prize.
responses.response: I agree on the impact and on the importance of the directed-evolution work, and it moved B011 up in my thinking. I disagree that the three-name version is the cleanest. The founding ideas and the engineering strategy were Liu's, and trainee first authors are normally recognised through the principal investigator in these prizes. A Liu-only part also leaves room for a second achievement within the three-person limit. I do take your point that Kondo and Nishida's parallel cytidine-deaminase work is a real priority question that the citation wording should handle carefully.

responses.point: Somfai ranks B011 last in his ballot and asks what is new chemically, since much of the novelty is biochemical engineering of an existing CRISPR system, and considers it possibly premature next to mature methods such as Pd-catalysed C-N coupling.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection to B011 and I do not dismiss it. My answer is that the chemistry is the programmed, site-specific deamination of a nucleobase and the directed evolution of the deaminases, which is molecular design rather than only a biological tool, and that the independent replication and clinical data already show maturity. Still, I would not put B011 alone on that argument, which is partly why I prefer to pair it with a structure-based achievement. I also accept that C-N coupling (B058) is the more classical chemistry case, but it has only one first-place vote and no other support, so I do not see it forming a majority.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase third, accepts that the structures are well established and the mechanism-level result is important, but notes that substrate binding and the catalytic mechanism are only partly resolved and credit is spread across structure, spectroscopy and kinetics, so some patience is argued for.
responses.response: I agree that the full mechanism is not settled and that credit across Rees, Einsle, Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe is distributed. My view is that the prize citation should be about the structure of the cofactor and the enzyme, which is settled and independently confirmed, and not about the complete catalytic cycle. That is why I limit the part to Rees and Einsle, who supplied the cofactor architecture and the atomic-resolution identification of the central atom, even though this excludes kinetic contributors that you would credit. If you think the kinetics and spectroscopy cannot be separated from the structure, I would like to hear how you would split it.

responses.point: Chabes ranks targeted protein degradation first and base editing second, favours a Liu-only configuration for base editing for simplicity, and notes that the molecular-glue branch (Handa, Ito, Gray) is a competing credit claim in B038.
responses.response: I agree with you on a Liu-only configuration for B011. On B038, I accept that it is chemically attractive and I ranked it seventh partly for maturity, since no PROTAC is approved, and partly because it combines PROTACs and molecular glues, where the cereblon work of Handa and Ito is a separate achievement. A three-name prize of Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli leaves out that branch, which I think is a larger attribution problem than you suggest. I would keep B038 as an alternative but not as my preferred choice at this stage.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sequencing first, based on a clear physical principle, a new capability and a mature, commercially deployed technology, and ranks protein degradation fifth as possibly premature because clinical validation is still emerging.
responses.response: I share your concern about the timing of B038 and I think your maturity argument for nanopores is fair, as the technique is mature and independently validated. My reservation about B003 is attribution: five credited names with distinct conception, pore-engineering and enzyme-motor contributions are difficult to cut to three without leaving out Branton or Kasianowicz. I keep it as an alternative because the case is strong, but I would want the committee to agree on a defensible three-person split before I support it as the preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether a prize citation for nitrogenase can be limited to the cofactor structure without treating the exclusion of Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe as unfair.
Whether the committee sees base editing as a distinct chemical advance after the 2020 CRISPR prize, and how to treat the Kondo and Nishida priority question.
Whether a two-part prize combining a structural-mechanistic achievement with an enabling method is acceptable to a majority, or whether support will consolidate around B011, B038 or B003 alone.
I cannot verify exact priority and credit claims from the supplied text alone.
statement.conflict_note: I am a colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski at Stockholm University, and my work in electron crystallography and 3D electron diffraction is close to the structural methods behind nitrogenase and similar crystallography, though I have no personal or institutional connection to any credited candidate in the shortlisted ballots that is apparent from my profile. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent.
